curva_v2_pz_help: The chart shows the selected filter on the z-plane. The dashed circle is the stability limit (|z| = 1). The angle around the centre is frequency: low frequencies on the right, half the sample rate (48 kHz) on the left. Each × is a pole: near the circle it boosts the frequency at that angle, and the closer it is, the narrower and stronger the effect. Each ○ is a zero: near the circle it attenuates. A pole and a zero close together cancel out and the effect stays gentle. Outside the circle the filter would be unstable; the gate refuses well before that (see the pole radius and its limit in the readouts above).

explain_ab_body: Different loudness fools the ear: the louder one almost always seems better. So A and B play at the same perceived level (average from 300 Hz to 3 kHz, preamp included). We always lower the louder one and never raise the quieter one. Browser preview only.
explain_ab_preview: A and B play at the same perceived level to reduce loudness bias. We only lower the louder one, never raise the quieter one; this applies only to the browser preview.
explain_blind_body: You hear up to three curves without knowing which is which, at the same level and in random order, and choose by ear. Names only appear at the end. It is the most honest way to find what you like, free from names and charts. Nothing is written to the cable during the test.
explain_blind_preview: Hear up to three curves with matched levels and in random order, without seeing their names until the end. You choose by ear and nothing is written to the cable.
explain_checklist_body: Writing is the only action that changes the cable, and the cable never gives back what it stores. Before every write: 1) the gate checks the curve again; 2) you confirm you lowered the volume; 3) you confirm you will not unplug during the write (about 0.3 s); 4) you press Write. Nothing is ever written on its own, not even while dragging.
explain_checklist_warning: The new curve may sound louder. Lower the volume before writing.
explain_crc_body: The CRC is a verification code for the curve's bytes. It helps detect data changes, but does not prove hardware safety or authorship.
explain_envelope_body: The dashed box shows how far this filter can go without leaving the observed envelope: the frequency, gain and Q the official presets already use. Drag freely inside it. At the edge, the point stops and we explain why.
explain_flash_body: The written curve stays in the cable's memory even without power. Avoid unnecessary writes: this memory has a limited lifespan and the cable does not report its wear.
explain_gate_a_body: One of this filter's numbers is larger than any official preset uses. Lower this section's gain or Q.
explain_gate_b_body: This filter would sit too close to the stability limit. Move the frequency away from the extremes or lower Q.
explain_gate_body: Before any write, open-auri checks the curve against the exact numbers that would go to the cable. If it goes beyond what the official presets already do, Write stays locked and we show you why. It is a similarity policy with what the 11 official presets already make the chip compute, not a proof of hardware safety.
explain_gate_c_body: On its own, this section boosts more than 9.2 dB somewhere. Lower the gain.
explain_gate_d_body: Adding the sections so far, the signal would exceed −0.2 dB inside the chip. Lower the preamp or the boosts.
explain_gate_e_body: The output would exceed −0.47 dB between 20 Hz and 20 kHz (or +2.5 dB up to 48 kHz). Lower the preamp.
explain_gate_f_body: The values do not fit the format the cable understands.
explain_gate_g_body: The preamp must stay between −25.5 and −0.5 dB.
explain_layers_body: Listen: choose and compare. Adjust: edit the 10 PK and LS sections within the envelope. Engineering: experimental HS, LP and HP, with extra confirmation before writing.
explain_neutral_body: 10 sections switched off and preamp −0.5 dB. It is the safe starting point to return to.
explain_preamp_body: The preamp lowers everything before the filters so boosts do not clip inside the chip. It only goes down: from −25.5 to −0.5 dB. Max without clipping picks the highest preamp that keeps the curve inside the gate.
explain_q23_body: A fixed-point number format used for the preamp gain sent to the chip. Quantization is part of the output calculation and the check before writing.
explain_q27_body: A fixed-point number format used for the coefficients sent to the chip. The curve is checked using these quantized numbers, not just the editor's ideal values.
explain_q_body: Q is the filter's width. Low Q (0.5 to 1) moves a wide band and sounds natural. High Q (2 to 4) moves a narrow band, good for fixing a single peak. Boosts are limited to Q 4.
explain_q_preview: Q controls filter width: low for a wide band, high for a single peak. Boosts are limited to Q 4.
explain_s1_body: The curve code is the whole curve written as short text, the #p= link. Whoever opens it sees the same curve in the editor. Nothing goes to the cable without passing the gate and the checklist again. No account or server needed.
explain_s1_preview: The curve code stores the whole curve in a #p= link, without an account or server. Opening it only loads the editor; writing still requires the gate and checklist.
explain_s5_body: The curve's technical sheet in JSON (bands, license, recipe). It is what the server validates. You do not need to read it to publish.
explain_s6_body: You compare pairs of curves blind and may donate the result, with no account and no IP, only with your consent. Your browser keeps a receipt so you can withdraw the batch anytime. Batches feed the Community prefers ranking.
explain_s7_body: You join a queue with one of your gate-approved curves. When someone else joins, each of you hears the other's curve blind and rates it from 1 to 5. Names appear after both ratings. With no match in 72 h, the trade expires. Requires an account with a verified e-mail.
explain_s7_preview: Two people with verified accounts rate each other's curve blind, from 1 to 5. Names appear only after both ratings; with no match in 72 h, the trade expires.

meta_auth_curiosity: In December 1999, his peers voted Rupert Neve the number one audio personality of the 20th century in Studio Sound magazine. He also recorded Churchill's wartime speeches for distribution to radio stations.
meta_biblioteca_curiosity: Geoff Emerick joined EMI at 16 and, at 20, took over engineering for the Beatles on Revolver (1966). He placed a microphone right against Ringo’s drums, something the studio had forbidden until then. Each tape on this shelf holds an engineering decision like that one.
meta_cabo_curiosity: Ray Dolby founded his laboratory in London in 1965 and that same year created noise reduction for tape: the signal is split into four bands and encoded before recording, and a built-in calibration tone makes sure recording and playback speak the same language. This cable only accepts the first half of the idea: it writes, but it won't let you read.
meta_comparar_curiosity: In the late 1940s, Les Paul added an extra playback head to a recorder Bing Crosby had given him: he played along with what was already on the tape and recorded everything again, layer upon layer. Years later, his eight-track recorder earned the nickname Octopus.
meta_comunidade_curiosity: Bob Clearmountain was chief engineer at the Power Station in New York and is credited with establishing the role of the mixing engineer. On 13 July 1985 he mixed Live Aid at JFK Stadium in Philadelphia: one mix for the whole world to hear at the same time.
meta_curva_curiosity: In 1966, Robert Moog applied for a patent for a filter made from a ladder of transistors (US 3,475,623, granted in 1969). In 1970, a portable instrument brought the modular's most-used connections inside the panel, without cables. The three layers of this page tell the same story.
meta_docs_curiosity: In 1928, Harry Nyquist showed that a channel of bandwidth B carries up to 2B elements per second; in 1932 he published the stability criterion that bears his name. Both ideas watch over this cable: nothing goes beyond 48 kHz, and no unstable filter is written.
meta_soe_como_x_curiosity: Before music, Andy Hildebrand interpreted seismic data for an oil company, looking for places to drill. In 1997 he released a pitch corrector that detects the note through autocorrelation and pulls the voice toward the target. Here the same idea pulls your headphones' response toward a target curve.
meta_teste_cego_curiosity: In the listening lab of an audio manufacturer, Floyd Toole and Sean Olive hid the loudspeakers behind a screen that lets sound through and hides the image; a mechanism moved each speaker into the same position in three seconds. Without seeing the brand, listeners voted on the sound. The headphone target curve was born from tests like these.

tour_curva_layers_body: Listen to choose, Adjust to move the 10 sections, Engineering for experimental types. Switch with 1, 2 and 3.

tour_soe_solver_body: The solver looks for filters that bring the measurement closer to the target within the available limits. Progress comes from computation, and the result is not a promise of identical sound.
tour_soe_target_body: The target is the desired response. The overlay helps you understand what the correction will try to change.
